theme: A Level Religious Studies - gospel of john
enonce_markdown: In the Prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-18), by which title is Jesus first described?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Distinguish the title of the Prologue from the titles that appear later in the Gospel.

### Solution

The Prologue opens by calling Jesus the Word, who was with God and was God, and who became flesh. The Good Shepherd and the True Vine are "I am" sayings, and the Lamb of God is the Baptist's title for Jesus in John 1:29, after the opening hymn.

theme: A Level Religious Studies - gospel of john
enonce_markdown: State **two** of the "I am" sayings of Jesus in John's Gospel.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Recall the sayings that join "I am" with an image.

### Solution

Any two of: "I am the bread of life" (John 6), "I am the light of the world" (John 8 and 9), "I am the gate" (John 10), "I am the good shepherd" (John 10), "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11), "I am the way, the truth and the life" (John 14), "I am the true vine" (John 15).

theme: A Level Religious Studies - gospel of john
enonce_markdown: John calls the miracles of Jesus "signs". Which one does he present as the first of them?

choix.texte: Turning water into wine at Cana.
The feeding of the five thousand.
The healing of the man born blind.

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Use the numbering given by the evangelist himself.

### Solution

John 2:11 calls the water turned into wine at Cana the first of the signs, through which Jesus revealed his glory. The feeding, the healing of the blind man and the raising of Lazarus come later in the Gospel.

theme: A Level Religious Studies - gospel of john
enonce_markdown: Which of these episodes appears in John's Gospel but in none of Matthew, Mark or Luke?

choix.texte: Jesus washing the feet of his disciples.
The agony in the garden of Gethsemane.
The feeding of the five thousand.

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Compare John with the other three Gospels, and discard episodes found in them.

### Solution

The foot washing (John 13) is unique to John. The Transfiguration and Gethsemane scenes are told in the first three Gospels, and the feeding of the five thousand is the one miracle told in all four Gospels.

theme: A Level Religious Studies - gospel of john
enonce_markdown: According to John 20:31, why was the Gospel written? Explain how the confession of Thomas (John 20:28) fits this purpose.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

State the purpose given by the evangelist, then show how an episode serves it.

### Solution

- **Purpose.** John says the signs are written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that through believing they may have life in his name.
- **Thomas.** Thomas, who had doubted, confesses Jesus as "My Lord and my God". This is the highest confession in the Gospel and echoes the Prologue's claim that the Word was God.
- **Link.** Jesus then blesses those who have not seen yet believe, a blessing that extends to the readers, so the episode models the faith that the Gospel hopes to produce.

theme: A Level Religious Studies - gospel of john
enonce_markdown: In John 11:49-52, Caiaphas argues that one man should die on behalf of the people so that the nation is not lost. Why is this described as irony in John's Gospel?

choix.texte: He openly confesses Jesus as the Messiah, but the crowd refuses to listen.
He knowingly lies to the Sanhedrin in order to protect Jesus.
He means a political calculation, but the evangelist presents his words as a prophecy that Jesus would die for the nation, so they are truer than he knows.
He quotes the Law of Moses to show that Jesus had broken the Sabbath.

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Irony in John means a speaker says more than he intends. Find the gap between the speaker's meaning and the evangelist's.

### Solution

Caiaphas intends to remove a threat to the nation under Roman rule. John comments that, as high priest, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation and to gather God's scattered children. The words mean more than he realises, which is the irony. The other options attribute to him a confession, a lie or a Sabbath argument that the text does not give.
